title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 8
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Agreeing What a Metre Is
passages.text:
A. Before standardisation, units of measurement were local, numerous and frequently defined by the object being measured rather than by an abstraction. A unit of land might be the area a team could plough in a day, which varied with soil and slope; a unit of cloth might differ between two towns a morning's walk apart. This was not disorder for its own sake. Units tied to the work they described carried information that an abstract number does not, and traders who dealt in both places simply knew the conversion.

B. The pressure to standardise came from taxation and trade rather than from science. A state levying duties across a territory with hundreds of local units cannot easily detect underpayment, and a merchant selling at distance cannot verify what was shipped. Both problems are administrative, and both are solved by a single unit whose definition is held somewhere central and cannot be adjusted locally — which is why the earliest standardisation efforts were enforcement projects with physical reference objects held under lock.

C. The eighteenth-century proposal that a unit should derive from nature rather than from an artefact was a philosophical claim before it was a practical one. If a metre were defined as a fraction of the earth's circumference, then no authority owned it and any competent surveyor could in principle recover it. The survey undertaken to establish that length took years, was conducted across a country in political upheaval, and produced a figure now known to be slightly wrong — which mattered less than the principle, since the resulting bar became the standard regardless.

D. Definition by artefact carried a defect that took a century to become pressing. A physical prototype can be damaged, and more troublingly it can drift: the international kilogram standard and its official copies diverged measurably over decades, and there was no way to determine which had changed, since the prototype defined the unit by definition and could not be wrong. A standard that cannot be checked against anything is not merely inconvenient; it makes the question of accuracy meaningless.

E. The resolution was to redefine units in terms of physical constants that are, so far as can be determined, invariant. Fixing the numerical value of a constant and deriving the unit from it removes the artefact entirely, and any laboratory with sufficient equipment can realise the unit independently. The change was designed to be invisible: the new definitions were chosen so that the size of each unit did not perceptibly alter, and no measurement anywhere needed adjusting.

F. What the episode illustrates is that a standard's authority rests on agreement rather than on nature, even when it is derived from nature. The constants were selected partly because they were convenient and well measured, and the numerical values assigned to them were chosen to preserve continuity with the artefacts they replaced. A system justified by universality was in its details shaped by the arrangements it inherited — which is the ordinary condition of standards rather than a flaw in this one.

passages.title: The Thin Layer
passages.text:
Soil is commonly treated as an inert medium that holds plants upright and supplies water and minerals. It is closer to an ecosystem than a substance. A handful contains more organisms than there are people on earth, and the structure that makes soil productive — the aggregation of mineral particles into crumbs with pore spaces between them — is largely built and maintained by those organisms and by the roots and fungi threading through it.

That structure is what degradation destroys, and it is destroyed more easily than it is created. Repeated cultivation breaks aggregates mechanically; the loss of organic matter removes the glues that hold them; and a soil whose crumb structure has collapsed becomes dense, drains poorly and admits less air. The visible consequence is erosion, but erosion is the end of the process rather than its beginning. A field can lose most of its productive capacity while still holding all of its soil.

Rates of formation and loss are the numbers that make the issue difficult to dismiss and are frequently reported carelessly. Soil forms slowly — commonly cited as centimetres per millennium, though the figure varies enormously with climate and parent rock — while loss under intensive cultivation on sloping ground can be orders of magnitude faster. Comparisons of the two are meaningful in direction and unreliable in precision, and the widely quoted global figures for years of topsoil remaining rest on assumptions their authors generally acknowledge and their repeaters generally do not.

The practices that reverse degradation are established and their adoption is slower than the evidence warrants, for reasons that are economic rather than agronomic. Reduced tillage, cover cropping between cash crops, rotations including deep-rooted species and the return of organic matter all rebuild structure measurably. They also impose costs immediately and return benefits over years, on land that in many systems is rented on short terms. A tenant farming a three-year lease has no mechanism to capture a benefit arriving in year eight, and no amount of demonstration addresses that.

Carbon has recently reframed the discussion and introduced a distortion worth noting. Rebuilding organic matter stores carbon, which has attracted funding that decades of erosion warnings did not, and this is welcome. It has also produced claims about the quantity of atmospheric carbon that soils could absorb which exceed what the measurements support, and a backlash against those claims risks discrediting practices whose agricultural case never depended on carbon at all.

The most reliable framing is the least dramatic. Soil is a slowly renewable resource being consumed faster than it is made, in a system where the people making the decisions frequently do not own the consequences. That is a problem of tenure, time horizon and price, and it is not primarily a problem of knowing what to do.

passages.title: The Road That Fills Itself
passages.text:
Adding capacity to a congested road reliably produces a reduction in congestion that is smaller and shorter-lived than expected, and in many documented cases the road returns to its former level of delay within a few years. The effect is well enough established to have a name — induced demand — and well enough replicated that its existence is not seriously disputed among transport researchers, though it remains counter-intuitive to nearly everyone else.

The mechanism is not that new drivers appear from nowhere. Traffic on a congested road is suppressed demand made visible: journeys that people would make are not made, are made at other times, are made by other routes, or are made by other modes, because the delay makes them not worth it. Widening the road lowers that cost, and each of those suppressed journeys becomes viable again. The new traffic is largely the same people travelling differently, plus, over longer periods, development that locates where access has improved.

The time structure matters and is usually collapsed. In the first months, journeys shift back from off-peak times and alternative routes, and the improvement is real and measurable. Over several years, people change where they live and work in response to the improved connection, and businesses locate accordingly. It is this slower adjustment that returns delay to its previous level, which is why studies with short observation periods find capacity expansion effective and studies over a decade generally do not.

Two misreadings of the finding recur. The first treats induced demand as an argument that road building is always pointless, which does not follow: if the additional journeys are valuable to the people making them, capacity has produced a benefit even where measured delay is unchanged. What the finding refutes is the specific promise of reduced congestion, not the broader case for access. The second misreading assumes the effect is confined to roads. Capacity expansion on public transport induces demand too, by the same mechanism, and this is generally regarded as a success — which reveals that the objection is not to induced demand but to what the induced travel does.

Pricing is the intervention that addresses the mechanism rather than its symptom, since a charge that varies with demand keeps the cost of the journey from falling to the point where suppressed trips return. Where it has been implemented, congestion has fallen and stayed lower, which is a stronger result than any capacity expansion has produced. It is also politically difficult in a way that building is not, because it makes an existing implicit cost explicit and assigns it to identifiable people at a stated moment, which is a different thing from the same people losing the same time in traffic.
